kf1.tip: Choose a meal you ate this week and say which of the five reasons for cooking (safe, flavour, texture, shelf life, variety) applied to it, and how.
kf1.note: A good answer names one real meal and links each reason you pick to a specific change in the food. For example, chicken is safe once its core reaches 75°C because the heat kills pathogenic microorganisms, and fried onion develops flavour as its sugars caramelise. Check you explained how, not just which. If you only wrote "safe" or "tasty" with no reason, the link is missing. Variety counts too if the method changed colour, flavour or texture.

kf2.tip: Sketch a frying pan, a pan of boiling water and a grill from memory, adding arrows to show conduction, convection and radiation at work in each.
kf2.note: Your frying pan needs arrows going up from the burner through the metal base into the food, showing heat passing by direct contact. The water needs a loop: warm water rising from the bottom and cooler water falling to replace it, which is a convection current. The grill needs straight arrows going down from the glowing element onto the top of the food, with no contact. If your water arrows only go straight up, you have missed the circulation.

cs1.tip: Stop stirring a béchamel sauce for five minutes: say what happens to the starch granules, the convection currents and the final taste and texture.
cs1.note: A strong answer covers all three parts. The starch granules settle at the bottom and scorch, because nothing keeps them suspended. Conduction keeps heating the base while the convection currents alone fail to heat the sauce evenly, so the top stays raw. The result is a lumpy, bitter sauce. If you only wrote "it burns", you have missed why: the uneven heating and the settling starch are the cause, which is why the spec lists the need for agitation.
